title: Punctuating Direct Speech
keyIdea: Direct speech is the exact words someone says, and inverted commas (speech marks) go round just those words: “Let’s go!” shouted Tom. The punctuation that ends the spoken words goes inside the closing mark. If the sentence carries on with said or asked, use a comma, a question mark or an exclamation mark, never a full stop, and said takes a small letter. If the speaker comes first, put a comma after said and start the speech with a capital: Mum said, “Time for bed.” Reported speech, like Tom said that he was cold, is not the exact words, so it has no speech marks.
familyTip: Take a comic or a picture book with speech bubbles. Pick one bubble and write it as a sentence together, with the speech marks round the bubble words and the name outside: “Can I come too?” asked Kim. Then swap it round so the name comes first: Kim asked, “Can I come too?” Check the capital letter and where the comma or question mark sits.

visual.caption: Exact words or reported? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Ben asked if it was lunch.
Jo said that she had won.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: bubble words into a sentence, place the speech marks, choose the mark inside, fix the slip, sort exact from reported speech.

kid: When we write what someone says, we use speech marks. They go round the exact words. In a comic, those words are in the bubble. “Let’s go!” shouted Tom.
The name and said stay outside the marks. Tom did not say shouted Tom. He just said Let’s go!
A mark always goes inside, at the end of the words. If the line goes on with said, use a comma, not a full stop. A question needs a question mark. Then said starts with a small s.

The name can come first. Then put a comma after said. The words in the marks start with a big letter. Mum said, “Time for bed.” Tom said that he was cold. Those are not his own words. So we do not use speech marks.
adult: Ages 7 to 10. The National Curriculum in England introduces inverted commas to punctuate direct speech in Year 3 and expects the full set in Year 4: speech marks, the punctuation inside them, a comma after the reporting clause and a capital letter to start the speech (English Appendix 2). CCSS L.3.2c and L.4.2b ask for commas and quotation marks in dialogue. Key words: direct speech, reported (indirect) speech, inverted commas, speech marks, reporting clause, quotation marks (US).

The rules: the inverted commas enclose only the words spoken. The punctuation that ends the speech goes inside the closing mark. When the reporting clause follows, a statement ends with a comma rather than a full stop, while a question mark or exclamation mark stays and no comma is added; the reporting verb then takes a lower-case letter (“Can I help?” asked Ava.). When the reporting clause comes first, it is followed by a comma, and the speech opens with a capital letter and ends with its own full stop, question mark or exclamation mark inside the closing mark.

Common mistakes: putting the comma or question mark outside the closing mark (“Come here”, called Dad); closing the marks round the whole sentence, reporting clause included; ending the speech with a full stop when said follows; capitalising said or asked after the speech; starting the speech with a small letter after Mum said; leaving out the comma after said; adding a comma after a question mark; and putting speech marks round reported speech such as Tom said that he was cold.

In the lab your child taps the words from a speech bubble inside a sentence, places the opening and closing marks in the gaps, chooses a comma, full stop or question mark for the box inside the closing mark, finds the one slip in a written line, and sorts exact words from reported speech. Every wrong move gets a reason. UK classrooms say inverted commas or speech marks; US classrooms say quotation marks. Both put this punctuation inside.

practice.prompt: Ella’s bubble says: Is it raining? Which words go inside the speech marks in: Is it raining? asked Ella.
practice.hint: Only the words in the bubble, the exact words Ella said, go inside.
practice.explain: “Is it raining?” asked Ella. The question mark belongs to her words, and asked Ella stays outside.

practice.prompt: A story has {n} lines of direct speech. Each line needs an opening and a closing speech mark. How many speech marks is that?
practice.hint: Count 2 marks for every line: one to open and one to close.
practice.explain: {n} lines with 2 marks each is {=2*n} speech marks.

practice.prompt: Which mark goes in the gap? “I like this book _” said Raj.
practice.hint: Does the sentence end there, or carry on with said Raj?
practice.explain: The sentence carries on with said Raj, so the speech ends with a comma inside the closing mark: “I like this book,” said Raj.

practice.prompt: {n} children write this line. Which way is right?
practice.hint: Look for a comma after said, a capital letter to start the speech and the full stop inside.
practice.explain: When the speaker comes first: a comma after said, a capital T, and the full stop inside the closing mark.

practice.prompt: Which sentence should NOT have speech marks?
choices: Sam said that he was tired.
practice.hint: Which one is not Sam’s exact words?
practice.explain: Sam said that he was tired is reported speech. Sam’s exact words were I am tired, so no speech marks are needed.

pool.hint: The comma belongs to the spoken words. Called Dad was not said.
pool.explain: The comma goes inside the closing mark, and called Dad stays outside: “Come here,” called Dad.

pool.hint: Think of a comic. What is inside the bubble?
pool.explain: Speech marks go round the exact spoken words, like the words in a speech bubble.

pool.hint: A question mark already does the comma’s job, and it belongs to Mia’s words.
pool.explain: The question mark goes inside the closing mark with no extra comma, and the line ends with a full stop.

pool.prompt: “I am hungry,” said Raj. Why is said spelt with a small s?
choices: The sentence carries on after the speech
Said is not an important word
pool.hint: Is “I am hungry,” the end of the sentence?
pool.explain: The comma shows the sentence goes on, so said is not the start of a new sentence and takes a small letter.

pool.prompt: A comic page has {n} speech bubbles. You write each bubble as a line of direct speech. How many lines need speech marks?
pool.hint: Each bubble holds one person’s exact words.
pool.explain: Every bubble is someone’s exact words, so all {n} lines need speech marks.

choices: Mia asked if she could play.
pool.hint: Asked if tells you what she asked, without her exact words.
pool.explain: Mia asked if she could play is reported speech, so it has no speech marks. Her exact words were Can I play?

pool.prompt: Kim asked, “Can I come too_” Which mark goes in the gap?
pool.hint: Kim is asking, and the sentence ends there.
pool.explain: It is a question at the end of the sentence, so a question mark goes inside the closing mark, with no full stop after it.

pool.prompt: Ben has lost his hat {n} times this week. Where does the opening speech mark go in: Ben asked, Where is my hat?
pool.hint: Find the first word Ben actually says.
pool.explain: Ben’s exact words start at Where, so: Ben asked, “Where is my hat?”

pool.hint: When said Raj comes after the speech, does the sentence end inside the marks?
pool.explain: Said Raj comes next, so the speech ends with a comma, not a full stop: “I am hungry,” said Raj.
